did_you_know.text: Did you know? The prophecy is dated to the first day of the third month, in the eleventh year, and is delivered to Ezekiel as the word of the LORD.
Did you know? The prophet addresses Pharaoh king of Egypt and his entire army directly, asking them, “Whom can you be compared to in your greatness?”
Did you know? In the central metaphor, Assyria is portrayed as a beautiful, towering cedar in Lebanon, with many branches and a crown rising high among the thick trees.
Did you know? The cedar’s greatness is attributed to the abundant water that nourished it: rivers and canals surrounded its planting and reached out to the trees of the field.
Did you know? The cedar symbolizes a power that offers protection: birds nested in its branches, wild animals lived beneath its boughs, and many nations dwelt in its shade.
Did you know? The cedar’s beauty and greatness were so extraordinary that all the trees of Eden in the garden of God are described as envying it.
Did you know? The turning point in the metaphor is pride: the cedar grew tall and its heart became proud because of its height, so punishment was decreed against it.
Did you know? After the cedar is cut down, its branches fall across the mountains and valleys, and the nations that had sheltered in its shade descend from it and abandon it.

Did you know? At the end of the prophecy, it becomes clear that the metaphor of the cedar is aimed at Pharaoh and all his army: they too will descend to the “lower earth” and lie among those slain by the sword.
